newsitem.title: USA: Ex U.S. FDA chief Kessler criticizes tobacco talks.
newsitem.headline: Ex U.S. FDA chief Kessler criticizes tobacco talks.

text.p: Former Food and Drug Administration Commissioner David Kessler said Wednesday that public health interests were not being served by the current tobacco settlement talks.
The goal should be "to try to reduce the number of people who smoke, and the number of people addicted, not how much money should be received," Kessler said in an interview.

In Chicago Wednesday, Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore said that the industry and state attorneys general had agreed on the public health issues, but that limiting industry liability was still a stumbling block to a final deal.
Kessler said he is not satisfied that the talks will get at the root of the tobacco problem, what he called children being seduced into picking up the habit.
He welcomed Wednesday's action by the Federal Trade Commission against R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co to prevent it using its cartoon "Joe Camel" advertisements to attract minors to smoking.
"There could not be anything that more personifies the targetting of young people than Joe Camel," Kessler said.

Kessler, who led the Clinton Administration's crackdown on the tobacco industry until leaving the FDA earlier this year, will keep a hand in the issue even as he assumes his new position as Dean of the Yale Medical School on July 1.
He will co-chair, with former Surgeon General C. Everett Koop, a new committee to advise Congress on the settlement talks and a national tobacco control policy.
The Advisory Committee on Tobacco Policy and Public Health's first meeting will be held June 5 on Capitol Hill.

The group includes representatives from the American Medical Association, American Cancer Society, American Lung Association, American Heart Association, the Society for Preventive Medicine, the National Medical Association, and the National Center for Tobacco-Free Kids.

Kessler said he stayed at FDA for six years partly to complete the job on tobacco that he began in 1991. He does not view tobacco as his life's work, but added, "it's not the kind of responsibility I walk away from."

Nevertheless, he is not optimistic he can convince Yale to divest itself of its tobacco investments. The school knew his views, Kessler said, but "the last thing anyone wants is me to give them investment advice."
